extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemaking stakeholders: regulated industry (power developers/utilities), state/federal regulators, and public commenters on emissions standards for new natural gas-fired combined cycle EGUs
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the EPA's criteria and supporting evidence used to determine that carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) is adequately demonstrated and meets BSER for new natural gas-fired combined cycle (NGCC) combustion turbine EGUs. Intended to guide rulemaking, permitting, and stakeholder comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90 percent CO2 capture demonstrated for NGCC
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA concludes that 90 percent CO2 capture from natural gas-fired combined cycle combustion turbines is adequately demonstrated as a performance level for CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by examples of planned and proposed commercial projects (e.g., NET Power projects, Sutter Decarbonization, Deer Park, Baytown), DOE-funded studies and demonstrations, and technical analyses. The EPA treats 90 percent as achievable over long periods (i.e., 12-month rolling averages) for base load combustion turbines under relevant flue gas conditions, variable load, and startup/shutdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence from coal-fired CCS projects to support NGCC CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations of CCS on coal-fired steam generating units provide further support that CCS on base load combined cycle units is adequately demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relies on the technical lessons and demonstration history from coal CCS (excluding EPAct05-assisted coal projects for certain legal interpretations) because many aspects (capture, transport, sequestration) are transferable; caveats noted about coal impurities not present in natural gas flue gas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flue gas composition and range of conditions acceptable for capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural gas combined cycle post-combustion flue gas composition is relatively uniform with generally low impurities; small differences (e.g., NOX) are not expected to adversely impact CO2 capture equipment operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many new units likely installed with SCR, producing uniform NOX; exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) can increase CO2 concentration and reduce O2 and volumetric flow, improving capture conditions. EPA concludes no substantial differences in flue gas conditions that would prevent achieving 90% capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turndown and variable-load operability of capture systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Single trains of CO2 capture facilities have turndown capabilities of ~50%; effective turndown to 25% throughput can be achieved using two trains of capture equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes capture rates can be higher at lower throughputs. Load-following operation is manageable (e.g., produce and hold additional lean solvent during off-peak hours to reduce auxiliary reboiler demand during peak hours). These factors support that capture rate is not affected by load following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Startup/shutdown strategies do not preclude high capture rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Startup and shutdown for NGCC units are fast (cold startups typically ≤3 hours; shutdown <1 hour) and do not adversely impact achievable CO2 capture rate when appropriate strategies are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several process strategies modeled to achieve 95% capture during startup: (1) reserve of lean solvent for startup, (2) dedicated heat storage for reboiler preheating, (3) fast starting steam cycle technologies or high-pressure bypass extraction. Amine solvents can begin capturing CO2 as soon as flue gas contacts lean solvent because natural gas flue gas needs less pretreatment than coal flue gas.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPAct05-assisted projects as corroborating evidence only
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EPA's interpretation of EPAct05, projects that received EPAct05 assistance may not serve as the sole basis for adequate demonstration determinations, but they may corroborate or support other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA uses EPAct05-assisted projects to provide additional support confirming that 90% capture from NGCC is adequately demonstrated, but bases the primary determination on other evidence as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 transport by pipelines adequately demonstrated
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 pipeline transport, as a component of CCS, is adequately demonstrated for use with new combustion turbine EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale mirrors that for coal-fired EGUs: pipeline network is expanding in the U.S.; CO2 delivered into pipelines is indistinguishable regardless of source; PHMSA comprehensively regulates safety of supercritical CO2 pipelines. New turbines may be co-located with storage sites to minimize transport. EPA considers permitting, rights-of-way, and pipeline build-out history and recent examples in its assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geologic sequestration adequacy and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Geologic sequestration (long-term containment of CO2 in subsurface formations) is well proven and adequately demonstrated as a component of CCS for new combustion turbine EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep saline formations, unmineable coal seams, and depleted oil & gas reservoirs are broadly available; EPA cites DOE/USGS/EPA analyses finding many states within 100 km of suitable storage. Regulatory protections include UIC Class VI well regulations (SDWA authority) and the GHGRP (CAA authority). EPA and states have permitting experience and processes to ensure secure storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic siting flexibility when local sequestration unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: If a region lacks suitable sequestration nearby, developers have two options: (1) site near demand and transport CO2 via pipeline, or (2) site near sequestration and transmit electricity to load (gas-by-wire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA expects project developers can balance siting to minimize long pipeline needs or to rely on transmission infrastructure. Examples (coal-by-wire/gas-by-wire) and RTO/ISO planning and historical multi-state generation arrangements support feasibility. EPA's geographic availability memorandum details the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of costs in BSER determination
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates the costs of CCS (capture, transport, sequestration) for new combined cycle units and compares them to other control costs to determine reasonableness for BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NETL baseline: 90% amine-based capture increases capital costs by 115% $/kW, heat rate by 13%, operating costs by 35%, derates unit by 11%; increases LCOE by 62% (27 $/MWh) and gives onsite CO2 reduction cost ~$81/ton. EPA notes reductions from 45Q tax credit, potential EGR, technological improvements, learning rates, DOE/IIJA/IRA funding, and other trends that lower future costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for technological options and innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA recognizes multiple capture technology categories (solvents, sorbents, membranes, cryogenic, molten carbonate fuel cells) and anticipates cost and performance improvements over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE-funded projects, commercial pilots, and research aim to reduce capital, operating, and auxiliary energy requirements. Learning-by-doing, supply-chain maturation, standardization, and research investments are expected to reduce costs and improve competitiveness of alternative capture technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) as a cost/performance modifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) can improve capture conditions (higher CO2 concentration, lower O2 and flow) and reduce costs for NGCC CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One study found EGR can reduce capital costs by 6.4%, heat rate by 2.5%, LCOE by 3.4%, and overall CO2 capture costs by 11% relative to no-EGR assumptions. NETL baseline costs referenced by EPA do not assume EGR, so EGR adoption could lower estimated costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projected cost declines via learning and policy support
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers historical and projected learning rates and policy incentives (e.g., 45Q, IIJA, IRA) as factors that reduce CCS capital and operating costs over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited evidence: studies showing 5–27% learning rates for related technologies; historical capture cost declines (e.g., $95/ton in older studies to ~$50/ton projected by 2025); NETL/NREL/DOE illustrative estimates (e.g., 25% capital cost reduction for Nth-of-a-kind facilities). Policy funding accelerates deployment and cost reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NETL CO2 transport and sequestration cost models
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relies on NETL 'Quality Guidelines for Energy System Studies; Carbon Dioxide Transport and Sequestration Costs in NETL Studies' and the CO2 Transport Cost Model for estimating pipeline and sequestration costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NETL model estimates single point-to-point pipeline costs including capital, related capital expenditures, and operations & maintenance. EPA references these tools for cost assessments and comparisons in BSER determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of commercial projects as supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific project examples (NET Power Allam-Fetvedt Cycle projects, Sutter Decarbonization, Deer Park Energy Center, Baytown Energy Center, Broadwing, planned West Virginia project, DOE-funded engineering/design awards) are cited as corroborative evidence that high capture rates and CCS deployment are viable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA lists project details (planned capture rates, technology vendors, FEED studies, permits, DOE selections) to illustrate commercial-scale deployment and to support the adequacy determination. These examples also show expected timelines (e.g., commercial operation dates) and permitting status (e.g., air permits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of differences between coal and natural gas CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA recognizes that natural gas post-combustion flue gas lacks coal impurities (fly ash, SO2, trace contaminants), simplifying flue gas handling and reducing solvent degradation and redundancy needs relative to coal CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical distinction supports the conclusion that achieving high capture (e.g., 90%) is, in some ways, more straightforward for NGCC than for coal-fired steam generators, and informs equipment/process design and cost expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation that most new base load NGCCs can be sited within 100 km of storage
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's geographic analyses conclude that the vast majority of new base load combustion turbine EGUs could be sited within 100 km of a sequestration site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE/USGS/EPA resource estimates and mapping indicate extensive deep saline and other storage options; EPA notes some states lack suitable geology but offers siting and transmission/pipeline options to address those exceptions.
